sections.h2: Who sets and collects property tax in South Dakota?
sections.html:
Three county offices do the work, and the state does none of the collecting. The county Director of Equalization values the property, the county Auditor turns the requests of each taxing district into levies, and the county Treasurer collects the bill.

The Department of Revenue's Property Tax 101 sheet says the state does not collect or spend any property tax revenue. Taxing districts include cities, counties, townships, school districts and special districts such as fire, ambulance, water and road.

If your question is about the value on your assessment notice, call the Director of Equalization. If it is about the bill, call the Treasurer. The department keeps contact lists for both on dor.sd.gov.

sections.h2: How is a South Dakota home valued and taxed?
sections.html:
A home is assessed at full and true value, which is its market value, as of November 1. The law then equalizes that value to 85 percent to get the taxable value, and the levy is applied to the taxable value.

Assessors combine three approaches for non-agricultural property: cost, market and income. The department says the market and cost approaches are the most common. Agricultural land is valued by a separate productivity formula.

The department's own example makes the math clear. A home with a full and true value of $120,000 has a taxable value of $102,000 after the 0.85 factor. A levy is expressed as dollars per thousand of taxable value, so at $10 per thousand a $150,000 value produces a $1,500 bill in the department's example.

DateWhat happens
November 1Legal assessment date
March 1Assessment notices mailed
March to JuneAppeal process
October 1Taxing district requests due to the County Auditor
NovemberAuditors calculate levies by November 1, and the Department of Revenue certifies them
January 1Tax bills mailed, and taxes due and payable

The department's example runs this way: a home assessed for the 2021 assessment year is valued as of November 1, 2020, and the taxes are payable in 2022. In other words, you pay on a value established the year before.

sections.h2: What is the owner-occupied classification and does it carry over to a buyer?
sections.html:
The owner-occupied classification lowers only the school general fund levy for a primary residence, and it ends when the house is sold. The department's July 2026 fact sheet says the status continues until the home is sold or its use changes, so the buyer has to apply again.

Other levies, such as county, city and school special education, are the same for every type of property. An owner can be a joint tenant, a life estate owner, a trust beneficiary or a contract for deed buyer, among others, and the dwelling must be the owner's principal residence.

  • Qualifying property: a house, condominium, townhome, manufactured home or a building of four or fewer family units.
  • One per person: an owner can claim the status on only one property statewide.
  • Deadline: the certificate goes to the Director of Equalization by March 15 of the current year.
  • Check your bill: an 'OO' or similar abbreviation on the assessment notice or tax bill shows the status.

The 2026 appeal guide lists the tests for appealing a denial: ownership and occupancy on November 1, 2025, that it is the only property you own with the status, that it is your principal residence, and that the certificate was filed by March 15, 2026.

sections.h2: When are South Dakota property taxes due, and what does late cost?
sections.html:
Bills are due January 1 and can be paid in two halves, by April 30 and by October 31. Under SDCL 10-21-23, the first half is delinquent May 1 and the second half November 1.

From the delinquency date, interest is added on the first of each month at the Category G rate set in SDCL 54-3-16. Taxes of fifty dollars or less must be paid in full by April 30. When the due date lands on a weekend, the tax is due on the last working day, and a payment postmarked by the last day before delinquency counts.

County offices add their own details, so read the treasurer's page for the county you are in.

  • Minnehaha County says taxes are delinquent May 1 and November 1 and a 10 percent annual penalty applies, described on the page as .83333 per month.
  • Brookings County does not accept partial payments for taxes that are due or delinquent, and in-person credit card payments carry a 2.5 percent fee.
  • Mead County's treasurer says delinquent taxpayers cannot pay online, returned payments carry a $40 fee, and a tax certificate sale is held in December.

sections.h2: What is the 2026 appeal calendar for a high assessment?
sections.html:
The first appeal goes to the local board of equalization, and the 2026 deadline to mail or file it was March 12. The Department of Revenue's 2026 appeal guide says you must appeal first to the local board or you lose your rights to the later boards.

Two groups skip that step: non-residents, who live outside the local board's jurisdiction, and owners in unorganized townships, who go straight to the county board. Some jurisdictions use a consolidated board, and your assessment notice tells you which applies.

The calendar moves each year, so use the guide for the current year. A written appeal can be a letter, an email or a signed PT17 form, and it needs your name, the legal description and a short reason. You also need evidence, such as sales of similar properties. Saying the value is too high is not enough.

sections.h2: What relief programs exist for owners, and how do they affect a sale?
sections.html:
The Department of Revenue lists several programs, and a few of them end or come due when the property is sold. The homestead exemption is the one sellers should know about because it defers taxes instead of removing them.

  • Homestead exemption: delays payment of property taxes until the property is sold. The taxes are a lien, and they must be paid with interest before the property can be transferred. The 2026 programs list gives age 70 or older and an April 1 deadline.
  • Assessment freeze: for owners 65 or older or legally disabled who own and occupy the home, stopping the assessed value from rising. Income limits apply, and the deadline is April 1.
  • Disabled veteran exemption: the first $200,000 of valuation is exempt for a veteran rated permanently and totally disabled, with a November 1 deadline. It lasts until the property is transferred or sold.
  • Paraplegic veteran exemption: exempts the property from all property taxes until transfer or sale.

The 2026 list also describes three legislative changes. SB 216 (2025) caps annual growth in owner-occupied valuation at 3 percent per county and local budgets at 3 percent, temporarily for five years. SB 245 (2026) uses sales tax revenue to lower school levies. SB 96 (2026) lets counties add a local sales tax of up to 0.5 percent to credit owner-occupied property taxes. The department's own note says layout makes some of those details hard to match, so confirm with the Property Tax Division at 1-800-829-9188, option 2.

sections.h2: What happens if taxes go unpaid?
sections.html:
South Dakota sells tax certificates on delinquent real estate, and the certificate holder can later seek a tax deed. Under SDCL 10-25-1, a tax deed proceeding is started after three years from the certificate sale and within six years of it, if the certificate has not been redeemed.

Anyone may redeem a certificate before a deed issues. Under SDCL 10-24-1, the redeeming party pays the treasurer the sum on the certificate, interest at the rate the property sold for, other taxes paid since then and interest on those. The treasurer records the redemption and gives a receipt.

That sequence gives an owner time, but the cost grows. The statutes do not set a fixed redemption price, so ask the treasurer for the current payoff. Mead County's treasurer publishes delinquent real estate in public notices before its December sale.

sections.h2: How are taxes handled when you sell?
sections.html:
Taxes follow the property to the county where it sits, and the county Treasurer is the office that can tell you what is owed. A homestead deferral, if you have one, is a lien that must be paid with interest before the property can be transferred.

The seller also pays the state's transfer fee, fifty cents for each five hundred dollars of value under SDCL 43-4-21. The Department of Revenue lists a Certificate of Real Estate Value form, PT 56, on its forms page, so ask the title company whether your deed needs it.

A cash sale does not change these steps. It only removes the wait for a buyer's loan, which helps if a deadline such as April 30 or October 31 is close. We buy houses in South Dakota as they are, and an offer has no obligation attached.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a high property tax assessment in South Dakota?
faqs.a: Start with your county Director of Equalization, who can explain how the value was set. If you still disagree, the first formal step is a written appeal to the local board of equalization by mid-March.

faqs.q: When are South Dakota property taxes due?
faqs.a: Bills are due January 1 and payable in halves, by April 30 and October 31. A half becomes delinquent the next day, May 1 or November 1, and interest then accrues monthly.

faqs.q: Does the owner-occupied status transfer to the buyer?
faqs.a: No. It continues only until the home is sold or its use changes, so a new owner must apply, with the certificate due by March 15.

faqs.q: Can I defer property taxes until I sell?
faqs.a: The homestead exemption defers taxes until the property is sold, for owners 70 or older per the 2026 program list. The taxes become a lien with interest and must be paid before the property can be transferred.

faqs.q: How long before a tax certificate becomes a deed?
faqs.a: A tax deed proceeding is initiated after three years from the certificate sale and within six years, under SDCL 10-25-1. Anyone may redeem before a deed issues.

faqs.q: Is there a statewide cap on assessment increases?
faqs.a: SB 216 (2025) caps annual growth in owner-occupied valuation at 3 percent per county for five years, according to the Department of Revenue. Check the department for how it applies to your county.
